segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate, a certain Tertullus, and they presented their case against Paul to the governor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul had been called in, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since reforms are being carried out for this nation through your foresight,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: in every way and in every place we welcome this, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But so as not to detain you any longer, I beg you, in your forbearance, to hear us briefly.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For we have found this man to be a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He even tried to desecrate the temple, and so we seized him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If you examine him yourself, you will be able to find out from him about all these things of which we accuse him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jews also joined in the attack, asserting that these things were so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the governor nodded to him to speak, Paul replied:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge for this nation, I make my defense with good cheer.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As you can verify, it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and they did not find me arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or anywhere in the city.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But this I do admit to you: it is according to the Way, which they call a sect, that I serve the God of our ancestors, believing everything that accords with the Law and everything written in the Prophets,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and having a hope in God, a hope that these men themselves also hold, that there is going to be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason I too always strive to keep my conscience clear before God and before people.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: After several years away, I came to bring gifts for the poor to my nation, and offerings.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I was engaged in these when they found me in the temple, purified, with no crowd and no uproar.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But some Jews from Asia—they ought to be here before you and bring their charges, if they have anything against me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: unless it is this one thing that I cried out as I stood among them: ‘It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Felix, who was rather well informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “When Lysias the commander comes down, I will decide your case.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard but to allow him some freedom, and not to prevent any of his own people from attending to his needs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as Paul discussed righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and replied,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “That is enough for now; go. When I find an opportunity I will send for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the same time he was also hoping that Paul would give him money, and so he sent for him quite often and talked with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and because he wanted to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in prison.

notes.note: The Greek word means a trained public speaker, and older English versions have 'orator'. In a courtroom setting it meant a professional pleader hired to present a case, so 'advocate' is used here. Most modern translations similarly have 'lawyer' or 'attorney'.

The same Greek word is translated 'nation' when it means a people as a unit, as here of the Jewish people (also verses 10 and 17), and 'Gentiles' when its plural means the non-Jewish peoples. English needs two words where Greek has one.

The word meant a school of thought or party, and Acts uses it neutrally of the Pharisees and Sadducees. It did not yet carry the later sense of 'heresy', though Tertullus plainly means it dismissively and Paul in verse 14 declines the label. The same English word is used in both verses so the echo can be heard.

notes.traditional: includes verse 7: 'and would have judged him according to our law. But the commander Lysias came and with great violence took him out of our hands, commanding his accusers to come to you'
notes.note: Some later manuscripts add a longer passage here, numbered as the end of verse 6, verse 7 and the start of verse 8. It is absent from the earliest witnesses and is omitted in the Greek text translated here, which is why the numbering passes from 6 to 8. Without it, 'him' in verse 8 is Paul; with it, the person Felix is to examine would be Lysias.
The ordinary word for a road or path is used in Acts as a name the followers of Jesus gave their own movement. Paul sets this name against his accusers' label 'sect'.

Most English versions have 'worship' here. The verb refers to religious service rendered to a deity, and it differs from the word translated 'worship' in verse 11, which refers to an act of homage. 'Serve' keeps the two distinct; some translations do the same.

notes.phrase: But some Jews from Asia—they ought to be here
notes.note: Paul's sentence breaks off in the Greek without a main verb, and the translation keeps the break. 'Asia' is the Roman province in the west of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city, not the continent. These were the people who started the uproar in the temple (Acts 21:27), and Paul's point is that the actual witnesses are absent.

The word is literally 'leader of a thousand' and was the standard Greek term for a Roman military tribune. Here it means the officer in command of the cohort stationed in Jerusalem. 'Tribune' is the more technical rendering used by several translations.

notes.phrase: his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish
notes.note: Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, whose death is told in Acts 12. According to Josephus, Felix persuaded her to leave her first husband, the king of Emesa, to marry him. Readers who knew this would hear a pointed edge in Paul's topics in verse 25.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here, addressed to a governor who sat as judge and who hoped for a bribe (verse 26), the word could equally be heard as 'justice'. The same family lies behind 'the righteous and the unrighteous' in verse 15, which older versions render 'the just and unjust'.

candidates.reason: It recurs throughout Acts 21–25 and in the Gospels and Revelation, and translations split between 'tribune', 'commander' and 'captain'; the rank should not shift between chapters.
It is frequent in the Gospels and Acts and rendered either 'council' or 'Sanhedrin'; readers should see one term for the same body.
It is rendered 'worship' or 'serve' by different translations and needs to be kept distinct from προσκυνέω across Acts, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation.
It is variously 'sect', 'party', 'faction' or 'heresy' across Acts, Paul and 2 Peter, and the neutral first-century sense needs one consistent treatment.
The traditional 'alms' is archaic, and modern options ('charitable gifts', 'acts of mercy', 'giving to the poor') vary across Matthew, Luke and Acts.

warnings: Verse 14: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
